transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it’s... it’s actually a bit hard to explain, but I guess what really brings me in today is that I’ve just gotten so incredibly slowed down lately. I mean, I'm an auditor, right? So my job is all about details and moving through these massive spreadsheets and workpapers efficiently. But lately, I’ll open a file, and I’ll just sit there. I’m not even kidding, I can sit there staring at a single audit workpaper for twenty, maybe thirty minutes before I even move my hand to type a single number or click a cell. It’s like my brain knows what I need to do, but my body just won't follow through, like I'm moving through molasses or something. And it’s not just a one-time thing; it’s happening all the time now. It’s gotten to the point where people at work have started noticing. My manager pulled me aside the other day to ask if I was feeling okay because I’m just not keeping up with my usual workload. I used to be able to knock out these audits so quickly, but now every little movement just feels so heavy and takes so much effort. I just sit there, staring at the screen, and the time just slips away, and I haven't accomplished anything. It's really starting to scare me, honestly, because I can't afford to lose this job, but I just can't seem to make myself move any faster.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time lately?

Sad and empty... yeah. Actually, empty is probably the best word for it. It’s... well, it’s hard to put into words exactly, but almost every single morning, most days really, I wake up and before I even open my eyes completely, I just feel this... this incredibly heavy, hollow feeling right here in the center of my chest. It’s almost physical, you know? Like a literal weight pressing down on me, but at the same time, it feels like everything inside me has just been scooped out. 

I'll just lie there under the covers, staring up at the ceiling, and I get this overwhelming sense that the day is already completely lost before I’ve even gotten out of bed. Like, what is even the point of trying to throw the blankets off, or get dressed, or log into my computer? The whole day just feels ruined and pointless from the very first second I'm awake. And it just stays with me, that emptiness. I'll sit on the edge of the mattress for I don't know how long, just feeling that hollowness, trying to find a reason to care about anything. I used to wake up and immediately start planning my morning, thinking about which client accounts I'd tackle first or what I was going to have for breakfast, but now... I just feel so hollowed out, like there's nothing left inside me to even care about the day ahead.
Do you find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?

Pleasure... no. Honestly, no, not at all. It’s actually really frustrating when I stop to think about it, because I used to be such an active person outside of work. I mean, my weekends used to be completely full of things I genuinely loved doing. I used to spend my Friday nights just planning out these really involved hikes. I'd pull up trail maps, check the elevation changes, figure out the best routes... and I’d always, always bring my camera. I loved taking photos, especially out in the woods, you know, finding the perfect lighting coming through the trees or taking macro shots of the leaves. It was my creative outlet, a way to decompress from all the spreadsheets. 

And then on Sundays, I had this whole routine where I would spend hours in the kitchen. I loved cooking on Sundays, trying out these complicated, time-consuming recipes that needed to simmer all afternoon, just filling the apartment with good smells. And on top of that, I used to volunteer at the local library. I’d help organize the stacks, or assist with the weekend community book sales. It made me feel so connected and, I don't know, useful to the world outside of my auditing firm. 

But now? Now... I don't even know. All of those things, every single one of them, they just feel like... like items on a tedious checklist. I look at my camera sitting on the shelf collecting dust, or I think about going to the grocery store to buy ingredients for a Sunday meal, and I just feel absolutely nothing. There's no spark, no excitement. It just feels like a massive chore that I’m being forced to do, and I just... I don’t care enough to even start. I've stopped replying to the volunteer coordinator at the library because the mere thought of going in just feels so heavy and exhausting. It’s like the part of my brain that used to actually enjoy life has just completely powered down, and now everything is just another exhausting task I can't bring myself to care about.
Do you often feel guilty about things?

Guilty? Um... I don't... I don't really know if I'd say guilty, exactly. I mean, I don't think I've done anything specifically wrong, you know? It's not like I'm sitting here agonizing over some terrible mistake I made at work or some horrible thing I said to a friend. I mean, sure, I feel bad that I'm falling behind on my audits, and I hate that my manager had to pull me aside, because I've always prided myself on being reliable. I've always been the person they could count on to get the workpapers done ahead of schedule. So, yeah, there's a little bit of... of disappointment in myself, I guess? But it's not this overwhelming, crushing guilt about my actions. It's more just this general feeling of being completely useless and empty, like I was saying before. I just... I don't really have that feeling of guilt that you're asking about. It's more just a profound lack of everything else.
How long have you been feeling this way?

How long... um. Well, let me think about the exact timeline, because it didn't just happen overnight, you know? It wasn't like a switch flipped on a Tuesday and suddenly I felt this hollowed-out feeling. But if I really trace it back to when this heavy, empty feeling really started to settle in and stay... it’s been about seven months now. 

Yeah, seven months. I remember because it started right around the time my husband’s company went through that massive downsizing. He had been there for almost five years, and we thought his position was totally secure, but then they just restructured the whole department. So he stopped working, and suddenly our whole routine was just completely upended. He was home all day, and I was trying to keep up with my audits, and the stress of going down to one income just sort of hovered over everything. 

At first, I thought I was just tired from picking up extra hours at the firm to compensate, you know? I thought, "Okay, I'm just stressed about the mortgage, I'm stressed about his job hunt, this is a normal reaction." But then the weeks turned into months, and he was still looking, and I just kept sinking deeper into this... this absolute lack of energy and interest. Even when things started to stabilize a bit, the feeling didn't leave. So, yeah, it’s been about seven solid months of waking up every single day and just feeling like the day is ruined before I even throw the covers off. Seven months of just dragging myself through the motions.
Have you ever thought about not wanting to live or had thoughts of suicide?

Suicide? No... no, I haven't. I mean, I know I just spent all this time telling you how empty and exhausting everything is, and how I can't even bring myself to pick up my camera or go to the grocery store, but... no, I don't want to die. It's not about wanting to end my life, it's more just... I don't know how to explain it. It's like I'm just existing, you know? Just taking up space. 

When I wake up in the morning and that heavy feeling hits me, I don't think, "I wish I were dead." It's more like, "I really, really don't want to do today." I just want to stay under the covers and let the world keep spinning without me having to participate in it. Because participating just takes so much effort. Even brushing my teeth feels like this monumental task that requires a pep talk. But actually taking steps to... to not be here anymore? No, I haven't had those kinds of thoughts. I don't have a plan or anything like that. 

It's strange, because my husband actually asked me something similar a few weeks ago. He noticed how withdrawn I've been, how I just sit on the couch staring at the wall instead of doing my Sunday meal prep, and he got really worried. He sat me down and asked if I was having dark thoughts. And I told him exactly what I'm telling you: I'm not thinking about hurting myself. I just... I just feel completely drained of life, even though I'm still technically living it. So, no, to answer your question, I haven't thought about suicide. I just wish things didn't feel so incredibly difficult all the time.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual, or have you had periods where you felt restless and couldn't sit still?

Moving slowly... yeah. Yeah, actually, that’s... that’s a really big part of what’s been going on. Restless, no, not at all. It’s entirely the opposite. It’s like... um... it's like I'm moving underwater, or through wet concrete or something. 

Actually, that's really what brings me in, to be honest. I've gotten just... so, so slowed down. It's affecting everything, but especially my job. I mean, as an auditor, you have to be sharp, you have to be quick, looking at multiple screens, checking balances, tracing transactions... and I used to be so fast at it. I could fly through a file. But now... I'll pull up an audit workpaper, right? Just a standard file that I've done a hundred times before. And I will literally just sit there. I'll sit at my desk, staring at this one single audit workpaper for... gosh, twenty minutes will go by, maybe more, before I even move my hand to type a single number or click the mouse. 

It's like my brain sends the signal to my hands to start working, and the message just... gets lost on the way. I just stare at the screen, and my body feels like it weighs a thousand pounds. And it's getting really embarrassing because it's not just me noticing it anymore. People at work have definitely started noticing that I'm not keeping up. I think I mentioned my manager pulling me aside earlier, and that's exactly why. They can see I'm just dragging. Even when someone walks by my cubicle and asks me a simple question, I feel like it takes me twice as long to just process what they said, open my mouth, and actually get the words out to answer them. It's just this heavy, sluggish feeling that I can't shake off, no matter how hard I try to force myself to just move like a normal person.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently?

Weight? Um... yes, actually. I have. And it's funny you ask that because I was just thinking about it the other morning when I was getting dressed for work. I have these navy blue pencil skirts that I wear all the time to the firm—they're just, you know, part of my standard professional rotation—and I put one on, and it was just hanging off me. It was so loose I actually had to go dig through the back of my closet to find a belt, which I never wear with those skirts because they used to fit perfectly. 

I haven't stepped on a scale to see the exact number, mostly because I just don't have the energy to care about the number, but I know it's a significant amount because none of my work clothes fit right anymore. And it's definitely not intentional. I'm not on a diet, I'm not trying to lose weight, especially with everything else going on. It's just... I don't have an appetite at all. 

Eating has just become this chore. It used to be something I enjoyed, you know? Like I mentioned earlier, I used to do Sunday meal prep, chopping vegetables, trying new recipes... but now, the thought of cooking, or even just chewing and swallowing, just feels exhausting. Food doesn't taste like anything. It's like chewing on cardboard. So I just... I skip meals without even realizing it. My husband will ask me what I had for lunch, and I'll realize it's 6 PM and I haven't eaten a single thing all day. When I do eat, it's mostly just me forcing down half a piece of toast or a few bites of whatever he put in front of me, just because I know I should eat something to stay alive. But the desire to eat is just completely gone, and yeah, the weight is just falling off because of it. It's just one more thing that feels totally out of my control right now.
Have you been feeling fidgety or had an inability to sit still recently?

Wait, fidgety? No, like I... I think I just mentioned a minute ago, it's actually the exact opposite of that. I'm not restless or bouncing my leg or pacing around or anything like that. I really don't have the energy to be fidgety. 

Like I was saying about work, the whole reason I'm here, what really brought me in, is how incredibly slowed down I've gotten. I'm the furthest thing from unable to sit still—I sit *too* still. I was telling you about my desk at the firm, how I will literally just sit there frozen, staring at one single audit workpaper for twenty whole minutes. Twenty minutes of just... nothing. Just staring at the monitor before I can even get my hand to physically move to the keyboard to type a number. 

So no, definitely not fidgety. If anything, I almost wish I had a little bit of nervous energy, you know? At least then maybe I'd be moving. But it's just this complete... standstill. And like I said, people at work have started noticing that I'm not keeping up. My manager, my coworkers... they see me just sitting there like a statue when I should be flying through these files. It's just so embarrassing to have them look at me while I'm trapped in this... this molasses feeling. So, yeah, no trouble sitting still at all. Sitting still is pretty much the only thing I actually *can* do right now.
Have you experienced any unusual thoughts or heard any voices that others couldn't hear?

Voices... um... gosh, I... I really didn't want to say anything about this because I know exactly how it sounds. But... yes. Yes, I have. 

It's... it's actually tied right back into what I was telling you about work, with the staring and the dragging. You know how I said I just sit there staring at the monitor? Well, sometimes, when I finally do manage to force my hand to click on something... like, if I open up a new spreadsheet to start a reconciliation, or even if I just click to open my email inbox... I hear this voice. 

And I don't mean like a loud thought, or my own inner monologue, or me just being hard on myself. I mean a crystal clear voice, like someone is standing right there in my cubicle with me. It sounds exactly like it's coming from just behind my laptop screen. And it always says the exact same thing. It says, "You missed it, they know." Just like that. 

The first time it happened, I actually physically flinched. I leaned over and looked behind my laptop, fully expecting to see one of the senior auditors or my manager standing there looking over the cubicle wall, because I'm already so hyper-aware that they're noticing how slow I am. But... I was completely alone. There was absolutely no one else in the room. No one walking by the aisle, no one in the adjacent cube. But the voice was just so real. 

And it keeps happening. Right when I open a spreadsheet or my email, it just speaks from that empty space right behind the screen... "You missed it, they know." It just makes that heavy, awful feeling so much worse, because I'm already terrified of messing up a client's file or losing my job because I can't think straight, and now I have this... this literal voice confirming all my worst fears when there isn't even a single person standing there. I just sit there looking behind the laptop like an idiot, but it's just the fabric of the cubicle wall.
Have you seen things that others couldn't see?

See things? No, um, no, definitely not. I haven't seen anything at all that isn't really there. Like I was just trying to explain with the voice... it's really just the hearing part. Honestly, if I started actually seeing things, I think that would be the absolute breaking point for me. 

But no, it's exactly what I was just saying a second ago—when I open that spreadsheet or click on my email inbox, and I hear that voice saying, "You missed it, they know," it sounds so incredibly real that my brain fully expects to see someone. I mean, the acoustics of it, if that makes sense? It sounds like a physical, breathing person is taking up space right behind my laptop screen. So I look. I always look. I'll peek around the edge of the monitor, or I'll even stand up a little bit in my desk chair to look over the top of the screen, just completely bracing myself to see one of the firm's partners or my manager staring down at me with this disappointed look on their face. 

But there's never anything to see. It's just my cubicle. I have this little blue pushpin stuck in the gray fabric wall right behind where my laptop sits—I used to have a little desk calendar hung up there but I took it down months ago—and every single time I hear the voice and look, all I see is that stupid blue pushpin. There's no one there. I haven't seen any shadows out of the corner of my eye, or visions of people, or anything like that. Just the voice coming from that completely empty space. And then I just sit back down and stare at the blue pin, trying to convince myself that my ears are playing tricks on me, because my eyes are telling me the truth: there is absolutely no one in the room. So, no, I haven't seen anything unusual at all. Just the voice.
Have you been feeling restless or having trouble staying still when you're not working?

Um... no, not at home either. Honestly, I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit here, but it really is the exact same situation whether I'm on the clock or off the clock. There is absolutely zero restlessness anywhere in my life right now. 

Like I was trying to explain earlier—and this is really the whole crux of why I finally made this appointment, what actually brings me in today—is just how profoundly, physically slowed down I've gotten. I know I already brought up the office, but that's where it's truly ruining my life, you know? It's the fact that I can sit there, at my desk, just dead-eyed staring at one single audit workpaper for twenty minutes... twenty literal minutes on the clock... before I can even muster the physical energy to move my hand to the keyboard to type a single digit. It's like my limbs weigh a thousand pounds. 

And it's the exact same when I'm not working. I'll go home and sit on my couch and just... not move. For hours. But at work, there are actual consequences, which is why it's so terrifying. People at work have actually started noticing that I'm not keeping up, my productivity has completely tanked, and they see me just sitting there frozen when I should be churning through these reconciliations. It's just this heavy, dragging sensation that follows me from my cubicle to my living room and back again. So, no, definitely no trouble staying still outside of work either. The stillness is pretty much the only thing I have going on.
Have you been feeling like you need to pace back and forth or engage in other restless activities when you're alone at home?

I... doctor, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here. I mean, pacing? Pacing back and forth? No, definitely not. Not at all. I don't mean to sound frustrated, but it's like I've been trying to say—this is the exact opposite of what I'm dealing with. I don't have any nervous energy. I'm not restless. I don't pace. I don't fidget. I don't do any of that. 

The whole reason I made this appointment, the absolute core of what brings me in today, is that I have gotten so incredibly, profoundly slowed down. It's like I'm moving through wet cement. I can literally sit at my desk, staring at one single audit workpaper—just a basic, routine reconciliation that I've done a hundred times before—and I will sit there for twenty solid minutes before I can even get my brain to tell my hand to move toward the keyboard to type a single number. Twenty minutes. Just frozen. And it's not just that I feel slow on the inside; people at work have actually started noticing. They can see that I'm just sitting there, staring blankly at my monitor, not keeping up with my billable hours, not churning through the files like I'm supposed to. My manager has been looking at me, they know I'm falling behind. 

And when I get home, it's the exact same thing. I walk through the door, I drop my bag, and I sit on the couch, and I just... stay there. I don't pace the living room, I don't get up to clean, I don't even get up to turn on the TV half the time. I just sit in the quiet because my body feels too heavy to move. So no, no pacing, no restless activities. Just this awful, dragging heaviness that I can't shake, whether I'm alone in my apartment or sitting in my cubicle.
Do you often feel worthless or blame yourself for things?

Worthless? I mean... I don't know if "worthless" is the word I'd use, exactly. I mean, I guess I just don't really think about it in those terms? It's more just... I don't know. I haven't really noticed feeling like that. 

I mean, sure, I blame myself when I actually mess up at work—like if I transpose a number on a balance sheet or miss a deadline, obviously that's on me, and I take responsibility for that. That's just being a professional. You have to own your mistakes in this field, or you're never going to survive busy season. But it's not like I'm sitting around blaming myself for, you know, the state of the world or things that have nothing to do with me. I'm just... I don't know. I haven't really been focusing on my "worth," I guess. I'm just trying to get through the day. So, no, I don't think I'd say I feel worthless or anything like that. Just... tired. And heavy. Like I was saying before.
Have you been feeling the need to engage in excessive movement or activity when you're alone?

Doctor, I really... I honestly feel like I am completely failing to communicate with you today, and I don't know how else to say this. We just talked about this. Excessive movement? Activity? No. The answer is no, and it has been no every time you've asked me some variation of this question. I'm sorry if I'm getting a little short, but it's just incredibly frustrating because it feels like you're looking for a completely different problem than the one I actually have. 

I don't have excessive movement. I don't have any movement. That is the entire problem. That is the whole reason I picked up the phone, navigated my insurance directory, and made this appointment to come see you today. What brings me in is that I have gotten so incredibly, physically, overwhelmingly slowed down. It's like my body is made of lead. I've told you about work, right? About how I can sit there, at my desk, staring at one single audit workpaper—just staring at the screen, looking at the columns, knowing exactly what I need to do—and I will sit there for twenty solid minutes before I can even get my hand to move to the keyboard to type a single number. Twenty minutes to just lift my hand. 

And it's not just a private struggle anymore. People at work have actually started noticing that I'm not keeping up. They see me sitting there like a statue when I should be working. My productivity is gone. And when I'm alone, like you just asked, it's the exact same thing. I go home, I sit down, and I don't move. There is no excessive activity. There's no activity at all. I am just... stuck. So please, can we move past the questions about pacing and moving too much? Because that is the absolute farthest thing from what I am experiencing right now.
Have you noticed any difficulty initiating movements or actions?

Yes! Thank you, yes. That is exactly what I've been trying to say. That is the exact issue—difficulty initiating. It's like there's a complete disconnect between my brain and my limbs. Like I was just saying, this is exactly what brings me in today. I have gotten so incredibly, overwhelmingly slowed down. 

I mean, I will literally sit there at my desk, staring at one single audit workpaper on my monitor... and I know exactly what needs to be done, I know the math, I know the client, but I will sit there for twenty minutes—twenty whole minutes—before I can even get my hand to move toward the keyboard to type a single number. It's like my brain is shouting at my arm to move, but the signal just gets lost somewhere along the way. I have to manually command every single muscle fiber to fire, and they just won't listen. It takes a monumental effort just to start the simplest physical motion, like reaching for my coffee or picking up a pen. 

And like I mentioned a minute ago, it's getting to the point where people at work have absolutely started noticing that I'm not keeping up. You can't really hide it in an open office when you're supposed to be churning through billable hours and instead you're just frozen in your chair. The senior auditors walk by and I'm just sitting there, unable to even lift my wrist to use the mouse. It's humiliating, honestly, because I'm a good accountant, I know how to do my job, but I just can't physically start doing it. So, yes. Yes, initiating movements is exactly the problem I'm having.
Have you experienced any periods where you felt like you were moving quickly or couldn't stop moving?

Doctor, I... I feel like we are going in circles here, and I really don't know how else to explain this to you. I'm trying to be patient, I really am, but you keep asking me about moving quickly, or pacing, or not being able to stop moving, and I keep telling you that is the exact opposite of what is happening to me. 

I don't have periods where I'm moving quickly. I don't have periods where I can't stop moving. I have periods—well, it's not even periods anymore, it's just my constant state of being—where I cannot start moving. Like I said just a moment ago, the whole reason I made this appointment, what brings me in today, is that I have gotten so unbelievably, physically slowed down. It's like I'm moving through molasses, or like gravity has suddenly tripled just for me. 

I told you about the audit workpapers, right? How I can sit there at my desk, in the middle of a busy accounting firm where everyone else is typing a mile a minute, and I will just stare at my monitor for twenty minutes. Twenty full minutes, just looking at a spreadsheet, knowing the deadline is looming, knowing exactly which keys I need to press, and I literally cannot even move my hand to the keyboard to type a single number. It's not a choice. It's like the connection between my brain and my muscles is just... severed. And I know I keep repeating myself, but it's because people at work have started noticing that I'm not keeping up. You can't just sit frozen at your desk during busy season and expect no one to see it. The partners notice. The seniors notice. My productivity is practically zero because I am so slowed down. So, no, I have never felt like I was moving quickly. I would give anything to move quickly right now. I can barely move at all.
Have you experienced any noticeable changes in your physical activity level, such as feeling like you're moving slower or faster than usual?

Doctor, I... I feel like I'm losing my mind here. I really do. I feel like I'm speaking a completely different language, or maybe the connection is bad, or... I don't know. I honestly don't know how many different ways I can say the exact same thing. Yes, I have experienced changes in my physical activity level. Yes. But it is entirely, 100 percent, without a doubt on the "slower" end of the spectrum. Never faster. Never, ever faster. 

I know I just said this, like, three times, but I'll say it again because it is literally the entire reason I am sitting here talking to you right now. What brings me in, the whole crux of this whole nightmare, is that I have gotten so incredibly, terrifyingly slowed down. It's not just a feeling of being tired. It's a profound physical heaviness. 

Like I told you, I am an auditor. My job is literally just looking at documents and typing numbers into a spreadsheet. It's not manual labor. But I can sit there, staring at one single audit workpaper—just one—and twenty minutes will go by. Twenty minutes of me just staring at the screen, knowing exactly what the numbers are, knowing exactly what I need to do, and I cannot even get my hand to move to the keyboard to type. It's like my brain is sending the signal, but the wires are cut. And I keep bringing this up because it's ruining my life. People at work have started noticing that I'm not keeping up. The partners, the seniors, they see me just sitting there, frozen. They think I'm slacking off, or daydreaming, or incompetent, but I'm not. I just physically cannot move my body at a normal speed anymore. So, yes, slower. Much, much slower. Never faster. Just... stuck.
Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy?

Yes... yes, I have. And I think it really ties right back into everything I was just saying about not being able to start things, because... well, I used to do so much outside of work. I used to be a really active, engaged person, you know? 

I would spend hours during the week just planning these intricate weekend hikes. I'd map out the trails, check the elevation gains, pack all the right gear. And I'd always take my camera with me because I loved taking photos—I used to be really into landscape photography, finding the perfect lighting and framing the trees just right. And then on Sundays, my whole routine was to spend the entire afternoon cooking. I'd go out, get all these fresh ingredients, and just spend hours in the kitchen trying out new recipes or meal-prepping for the week. It was my way to unwind. And on top of all that, I even used to volunteer at the local library. I loved being there, organizing the stacks, helping people find what they were looking for. 

But now... now, I don't do any of it. None of it. It's not even that I actively decided I hate those things suddenly, it's just that... the thought of doing them is completely exhausting. I look at my camera sitting on the shelf, or I think about looking up a recipe for Sunday, and those things just feel like items on a massive, overwhelming checklist that I just don't care enough to even attempt to start. The joy is just completely drained out of them. They just feel like more work, more things I have to force my body to do. So I don't. I just sit there, just like I do at my desk with those workpapers, not caring and not moving.
Have you had thoughts of suicide without having a plan to act on them?

No... no, I haven't. I mean, I know things are bad. I know I'm sitting here telling you that I can't move, that I can't do my job, that I can't even get myself to go for a walk or cook a meal anymore. And it's miserable, it really is. It feels like I'm just existing in this heavy, gray fog where everything is just so hard and pointless. But... I don't want to die. 

I haven't had thoughts like that. I haven't sat there thinking about ending it all, or wishing I wouldn't wake up, or anything along those lines. Even when I'm staring at that monitor for twenty minutes, completely frozen, feeling like an absolute failure because I can't even type a number into a cell... my brain doesn't go to suicide. It just goes to... how am I going to get through the next hour? How am I going to explain this to the senior auditor? How am I going to get up and go to the bathroom when my legs feel like lead? 

So, no. I don't have those thoughts. I don't have a plan, I don't have the urge... I just want to feel normal again. I just want to be able to move and care about things. But dying isn't... that's not something I'm thinking about.

patient.answer:
Yes! Thank you, yes. That is exactly what I've been trying to say. That is the exact issue—difficulty initiating. It's like there's a complete disconnect between my brain and my limbs. Like I was just saying, this is exactly what brings me in today. I have gotten so incredibly, overwhelmingly slowed down. 

I mean, I will literally sit there at my desk, staring at one single audit workpaper on my monitor... and I know exactly what needs to be done, I know the math, I know the client, but I will sit there for twenty minutes—twenty whole minutes—before I can even get my hand to move toward the keyboard to type a single number. It's like my brain is shouting at my arm to move, but the signal just gets lost somewhere along the way. I have to manually command every single muscle fiber to fire, and they just won't listen. It takes a monumental effort just to start the simplest physical motion, like reaching for my coffee or picking up a pen. 

And like I mentioned a minute ago, it's getting to the point where people at work have absolutely started noticing that I'm not keeping up. You can't really hide it in an open office when you're supposed to be churning through billable hours and instead you're just frozen in your chair. The senior auditors walk by and I'm just sitting there, unable to even lift my wrist to use the mouse. It's humiliating, honestly, because I'm a good accountant, I know how to do my job, but I just can't physically start doing it. So, yes. Yes, initiating movements is exactly the problem I'm having.

doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods where you felt like you were moving quickly or couldn't stop moving?

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I feel like we are going in circles here, and I really don't know how else to explain this to you. I'm trying to be patient, I really am, but you keep asking me about moving quickly, or pacing, or not being able to stop moving, and I keep telling you that is the exact opposite of what is happening to me. 

I don't have periods where I'm moving quickly. I don't have periods where I can't stop moving. I have periods—well, it's not even periods anymore, it's just my constant state of being—where I cannot start moving. Like I said just a moment ago, the whole reason I made this appointment, what brings me in today, is that I have gotten so unbelievably, physically slowed down. It's like I'm moving through molasses, or like gravity has suddenly tripled just for me. 

I told you about the audit workpapers, right? How I can sit there at my desk, in the middle of a busy accounting firm where everyone else is typing a mile a minute, and I will just stare at my monitor for twenty minutes. Twenty full minutes, just looking at a spreadsheet, knowing the deadline is looming, knowing exactly which keys I need to press, and I literally cannot even move my hand to the keyboard to type a single number. It's not a choice. It's like the connection between my brain and my muscles is just... severed. And I know I keep repeating myself, but it's because people at work have started noticing that I'm not keeping up. You can't just sit frozen at your desk during busy season and expect no one to see it. The partners notice. The seniors notice. My productivity is practically zero because I am so slowed down. So, no, I have never felt like I was moving quickly. I would give anything to move quickly right now. I can barely move at all.

doctor.question: Have you experienced any noticeable changes in your physical activity level, such as feeling like you're moving slower or faster than usual?

target_item.name: Psychomotor_Changes
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I’ve gotten so slowed down that I can sit staring at one audit workpaper for twenty minutes before I even move my hand to type, and people at work have started noticing I’m not keeping up.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about noticeable changes in physical activity level, specifically whether I feel like I'm moving slower or faster than usual, which directly addresses psychomotor changes.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I feel like I'm losing my mind here. I really do. I feel like I'm speaking a completely different language, or maybe the connection is bad, or... I don't know. I honestly don't know how many different ways I can say the exact same thing. Yes, I have experienced changes in my physical activity level. Yes. But it is entirely, 100 percent, without a doubt on the "slower" end of the spectrum. Never faster. Never, ever faster. 

I know I just said this, like, three times, but I'll say it again because it is literally the entire reason I am sitting here talking to you right now. What brings me in, the whole crux of this whole nightmare, is that I have gotten so incredibly, terrifyingly slowed down. It's not just a feeling of being tired. It's a profound physical heaviness. 

Like I told you, I am an auditor. My job is literally just looking at documents and typing numbers into a spreadsheet. It's not manual labor. But I can sit there, staring at one single audit workpaper—just one—and twenty minutes will go by. Twenty minutes of me just staring at the screen, knowing exactly what the numbers are, knowing exactly what I need to do, and I cannot even get my hand to move to the keyboard to type. It's like my brain is sending the signal, but the wires are cut. And I keep bringing this up because it's ruining my life. People at work have started noticing that I'm not keeping up. The partners, the seniors, they see me just sitting there, frozen. They think I'm slacking off, or daydreaming, or incompetent, but I'm not. I just physically cannot move my body at a normal speed anymore. So, yes, slower. Much, much slower. Never faster. Just... stuck.

doctor.question: Have you lost interest in activities you used to enjoy?

target_item.name: Loss_of_Interest
target_item.manifestation: I used to plan hikes, take photos, cook on Sundays, and volunteer at the library, but now those things just feel like items on a checklist I don’t care enough to start.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking if I have lost interest in activities I used to enjoy, which corresponds to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Yes... yes, I have. And I think it really ties right back into everything I was just saying about not being able to start things, because... well, I used to do so much outside of work. I used to be a really active, engaged person, you know? 

I would spend hours during the week just planning these intricate weekend hikes. I'd map out the trails, check the elevation gains, pack all the right gear. And I'd always take my camera with me because I loved taking photos—I used to be really into landscape photography, finding the perfect lighting and framing the trees just right. And then on Sundays, my whole routine was to spend the entire afternoon cooking. I'd go out, get all these fresh ingredients, and just spend hours in the kitchen trying out new recipes or meal-prepping for the week. It was my way to unwind. And on top of all that, I even used to volunteer at the local library. I loved being there, organizing the stacks, helping people find what they were looking for. 

But now... now, I don't do any of it. None of it. It's not even that I actively decided I hate those things suddenly, it's just that... the thought of doing them is completely exhausting. I look at my camera sitting on the shelf, or I think about looking up a recipe for Sunday, and those things just feel like items on a massive, overwhelming checklist that I just don't care enough to even attempt to start. The joy is just completely drained out of them. They just feel like more work, more things I have to force my body to do. So I don't. I just sit there, just like I do at my desk with those workpapers, not caring and not moving.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of suicidal thoughts without a plan
doctor.question: Have you had thoughts of suicide without having a plan to act on them?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about suicidal thoughts or ideation, which is not covered in my provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No... no, I haven't. I mean, I know things are bad. I know I'm sitting here telling you that I can't move, that I can't do my job, that I can't even get myself to go for a walk or cook a meal anymore. And it's miserable, it really is. It feels like I'm just existing in this heavy, gray fog where everything is just so hard and pointless. But... I don't want to die. 

I haven't had thoughts like that. I haven't sat there thinking about ending it all, or wishing I wouldn't wake up, or anything along those lines. Even when I'm staring at that monitor for twenty minutes, completely frozen, feeling like an absolute failure because I can't even type a number into a cell... my brain doesn't go to suicide. It just goes to... how am I going to get through the next hour? How am I going to explain this to the senior auditor? How am I going to get up and go to the bathroom when my legs feel like lead? 

So, no. I don't have those thoughts. I don't have a plan, I don't have the urge... I just want to feel normal again. I just want to be able to move and care about things. But dying isn't... that's not something I'm thinking about.
